Apocalyptic Measurements
uh-pok-uh-LIP-tik MEZH-er-ments
noun phrase (the symbolic numbers of Revelation)
From “apocalyptic” (Greek apokalypsis, an unveiling) and “measurements”; the symbolic dimensions and numbers given in the Revelation, as the measuring of the city and temple.

Biblical Definition

Apocalyptic measurements are the symbolic dimensions and numbers given in the Revelation—the measuring of the temple, the city foursquare of twelve thousand furlongs, the wall of a hundred forty and four cubits—which convey spiritual truth through significant figures rather than mere surveyor's data. An angel with a golden reed measures the new Jerusalem, and the city lieth foursquare, its length, breadth, and height equal: a perfect cube, recalling the holy of holies, the dwelling of God now enlarging to embrace all His people. The wall is a hundred forty and four cubits, twelve times twelve, the number of the tribes and the apostles multiplied—the fulness of the covenant people. John is given a reed to measure the temple of God and them that worship therein, a sign of God's preservation and ownership of His true worshippers. The dictionary holds that these measurements are to be read as the apocalyptic genre intends: numerically symbolic, freighted with meaning—twelve for the covenant people, the cube for the divine presence, perfect dimensions for the perfected church—not as literal architectural specifications for a future structure. The act of measuring itself signifies divine ownership, protection, and the certainty of God's purpose. The dictionary marks this against two errors: the wooden literalism that turns the figures into blueprints for a rebuilt temple or a calculable city, missing the symbolism the genre demands; and the dismissive spiritualism that empties the numbers of any real meaning. Read aright, the apocalyptic measurements declare that God knows, owns, protects, and perfects His people, and that the city He builds for them is laid out by His own hand in the perfect proportions of His presence.

Webster 1828 Definition

The symbolic dimensions and numbers of the Revelation—the foursquare city of twelve thousand furlongs, the wall of 144 cubits, the measuring of the temple—conveying spiritual truth through significant figures, not literal blueprints.

APOCALYPTIC MEASUREMENTS, noun phrase. The symbolic dimensions and numbers of the Revelation.

The city lieth foursquare, twelve thousand furlongs, length, breadth, and height equal (Revelation 21:16).

The wall is a hundred forty and four cubits—twelve times twelve (Revelation 21:17).

John is given a reed to measure the temple and them that worship therein (Revelation 11:1).

Numerically symbolic—the cube of God's presence, the twelve of His people—not literal blueprints.

Key Scripture

Re 21:16 — "And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal."

Re 21:17 — "And he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel."

Re 11:1 — "And there was given me a reed like unto a rod: and the angel stood, saying, Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship therein."

Re 21:15 — "And he that talked with me had a golden reed to measure the city, and the gates thereof, and the wall thereof."

Modern Corruption

Wooden literalism turns the figures into blueprints for a rebuilt temple or a calculable city, while dismissive spiritualism empties the numbers of all meaning; both miss the symbolism the apocalyptic genre demands.

expand to see more

The literalist error, common in dispensational prophecy teaching, treats the apocalyptic measurements as architectural specifications—calculating the cubits of a future temple or the miles of a literal cubic city floating above the earth. The dictionary regards this as a misreading of the genre. Apocalyptic literature speaks in significant numbers and figures: twelve for the covenant people, a hundred forty-four for their fulness, the cube for the holy of holies where God dwells. To reduce these to a builder's plan is to trade the rich symbolism the Spirit intended for a wooden literalism the text does not bear.

The opposite error so spiritualizes the figures that they mean nothing definite at all, a vague gesture toward heaven with no content. But the numbers are precise and purposeful: the perfect cube declares that the whole city is now the dwelling-place of God, the twelves declare it the home of the covenant people, and the act of measuring declares God's ownership and protection of His own. The dictionary holds the apocalyptic measurements as genuine revelation in symbolic dress—teaching that God knows, owns, guards, and perfects His people, and builds for them a city of perfect proportions, the eternal dwelling of His presence.

Hebrew Roots

From apokalypsis (an unveiling) and the measuring imagery of the Revelation; the “reed” (Greek kalamos) and the numbers twelve and its multiples carry the symbolism.

expand to see more

Apokalypsis, Greek, an unveiling or revelation, the genre of symbolic vision.

Kalamos, Greek, a reed or measuring-rod, the angel's instrument.

Twelve and its multiples (144; 12,000) signify the fulness of the covenant people.

The “foursquare” cube recalls the holy of holies, the dwelling of God.

The act of measuring signifies divine ownership, protection, and sure purpose.

Usage

"The teacher read the foursquare city as the symbol of God's dwelling enlarged to His whole people, not a literal cube."

"He warned against turning the apocalyptic measurements into blueprints for a rebuilt temple."

"She saw in the measuring of the temple the LORD's ownership and protection of His true worshippers."
